original_question: Is the set of countable graphs G on ω that are isomorphic to their complement graphs G^c a Borel set?
target_in_paper: Section 10 (Su Gao), Problem 32 (“The graph complement problem”), with Theorem 33 providing the answer.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the exact target of the paper very closely: it is about graphs on the fixed vertex set ω, the condition that a graph be isomorphic to its complement, and the descriptive-set-theoretic question of whether the resulting class is Borel. This is essentially Problem 32.
missing_details: The ambient coding space should be stated explicitly: the class is viewed as a subset of 2^{ω×ω}.
The complement graph must be defined exactly as in the paper: G^c = { (m,n) ∈ ω×ω : m ≠ n and (m,n) ∉ G }, so the diagonal is excluded.
To make the question fully stand-alone, “graph on ω” should be unpacked as an ordinary graph coded on the fixed domain ω, i.e. an irreflexive symmetric relation on ω.
The meaning of G ≅ G^c should be explicit: there is a bijection of ω carrying the edge relation of G to that of G^c.
It should be kept clear that this is the undirected-graph version only; the paper treats directed graphs and tournaments separately in a later theorem.
refined_question: In the Polish space 2^{ω×ω}, is the set { G ∈ 2^{ω×ω} : G is an irreflexive symmetric relation on ω and G ≅ G^c }, where G^c = { (m,n) ∈ ω×ω : m ≠ n and (m,n) ∉ G }, a Borel subset?
justification: The draft is already nearly verbatim to Problem 32 in Section 10, which asks whether the class of graphs on ω that are isomorphic to their complements is Borel. The nearby context supplies the exact definition of the complement graph, and Theorem 33 shows that this precise set is not merely non-Borel but Sigma^1_1-complete. Theorem 34 then separately lists directed-graph and tournament variants, confirming that Problem 32 is specifically about ordinary undirected graphs and should not be broadened.
